pos: n. (proper name; a son of Aram in the Table of Nations)
etymology: Hebrew Gether, of uncertain meaning; some connect it with a word for fear or for a press.
biblical_def: Gether is the third son of Aram in the Table of Nations: “And the children of Aram; Uz, and Hul, and Gether, and Mash” (Genesis 10:23). Aram is the father of the Aramean peoples, the Syrians of the Old Testament, and Gether stands for a branch of them whose later history Scripture does not trace. The Chronicler repeats the line in a compressed form, listing Aram's sons straight after Shem's (1 Chronicles 1:17). The value of the name lies in the chapter that holds it. Genesis 10 refuses to begin the history of salvation with Abraham alone; it first sets every people under heaven in a single family descended from Noah, “and by these were the nations divided in the earth after the flood” (Genesis 10:32). Paul preached the same truth at Athens: God “hath made of one blood all nations of men” (Acts 17:26). Gether is one of those nations, named and then left, but never outside the reckoning of the God who divided the earth.

corruption_summary: The Table of Nations is read as ancient ethnic propaganda; Scripture uses it to establish the one blood and common accountability of every people.
corruption_paragraphs: Critics often treat Genesis 10 as a map of political alliances projected back into a fictional family tree. Its plain purpose is the opposite of tribal pride: every people, including Israel's enemies, is placed within one family under one God, before Abraham is so much as named.

The principle to recover is the unity of the human race. Paul grounds the gospel's universal call on it at Athens. Neither racial supremacy nor the modern dissolution of nations into mere constructs survives Genesis 10: the nations are real, distinct, and of one blood.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Aram in the Table of Nations)
etymology: Hebrew Chul, perhaps circle or writhing, from chul, to whirl, to writhe.
biblical_def: Hul is the second son of Aram: “And the children of Aram; Uz, and Hul, and Gether, and Mash” (Genesis 10:23). He is the eponym of an Aramean people whose territory is not fixed by Scripture; older writers placed it near the waters of Merom or in Armenia, but the text itself is silent. His brother Uz gave his name to the land where Job lived, so the line of Hul sits beside the most famous Gentile believer of the Old Testament. The Chronicler, compressing the record, counts Aram's sons with Shem's own (1 Chronicles 1:17). Hul matters as one of the threads in the single fabric of Genesis 10, the chapter that declares every nation a branch of Noah's family and every boundary a matter of God's determination, the ground on which the gospel was later preached to all nations alike.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Joktan, father of a people of southern Arabia)
etymology: Hebrew Chatsarmaveth, court of death or village of death, from chatser, court, enclosure, and maveth, death.
biblical_def: Hazarmaveth is the third son of Joktan: “And Joktan begat Almodad, and Sheleph, and Hazarmaveth, and Jerah” (Genesis 10:26). Joktan was the brother of Peleg, “for in his days was the earth divided” (Genesis 10:25), and his thirteen sons settled the south of Arabia, “from Mesha, as thou goest unto Sephar a mount of the east” (Genesis 10:30). Hazarmaveth's name survives in the region still called Hadramaut on the southern coast of the Arabian peninsula, one of the clearest cases where a name in the Table of Nations persists in a modern place-name. The meaning, court of death, is grim, and fits a hot and harsh country. Its significance is that Peleg's brother's line went south and east, away from the line of promise, while Peleg's line led to Abraham; yet the same chapter keeps both, and the gospel would come to Arabia in its time.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother)
etymology: Hebrew Chazo, vision, from chazah, to see, to behold.
biblical_def: Hazo is the fifth of the eight sons Milcah bore to Nahor: “And Chesed, and Hazo, and Pildash, and Jidlaph, and Bethuel” (Genesis 22:22). The list is introduced by news brought to Abraham just after the binding of Isaac on Moriah: “Behold, Milcah, she hath also born children unto thy brother Nahor” (Genesis 22:20). The placement is deliberate. Abraham has just received Isaac back from the altar, and the very next thing the text records is the family in Haran from which Isaac's wife will come, for the list ends, “And Bethuel begat Rebekah” (Genesis 22:23). Hazo is a brother of Rebekah's father, a branch of the family that stayed in Mesopotamia. Nothing more is told of him. His name, vision, fits a chapter about the LORD who sees and provides, though he himself had no part in the promise his uncle carried.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Nahor by his concubine Reumah)
etymology: Hebrew Gacham, perhaps flame or burning; the meaning is uncertain.
biblical_def: Gaham is one of the four sons born to Nahor, Abraham's brother, by his concubine: “And his concubine, whose name was Reumah, she bare also Tebah, and Gaham, and Thahash, and Maachah” (Genesis 22:24). With Milcah's eight sons this makes twelve, the same number as the sons of Ishmael and the sons of Jacob, and the parallel is not accidental: Genesis repeatedly shows nations of twelve tribes rising from the patriarchal family, while only one line carries the promise. Nahor's twelve stayed in Aram; Ishmael's twelve became princes in the desert; Jacob's twelve became Israel. Gaham's name is recorded and nothing more. The careful distinction between the sons of the wife and the sons of the concubine anticipates Abraham's own household, where the sons of the concubines received gifts and were sent away eastward, while Isaac inherited all.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Midian, grandson of Abraham by Keturah)
etymology: Hebrew 'Elda'ah, God has called or God of knowledge, from 'el, God, and yada', to know.
biblical_def: Eldaah is the fifth son of Midian: “And the sons of Midian; Ephah, and Epher, and Hanoch, and Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the children of Keturah” (Genesis 25:4). Midian was a son of Abraham by Keturah, the wife he took after Sarah's death, and his sons became the Midianite clans. Abraham's dealing with them is recorded in a single sentence: “unto the sons of the concubines, which Abraham had, Abraham gave gifts, and sent them away from Isaac his son, while he yet lived, eastward, unto the east country” (Genesis 25:6). The descendants of Eldaah and his brothers return to the story as Midian, sometimes ally and sometimes oppressor: Jethro the priest of Midian, the Midianite seducers at Peor, the hordes Gideon routed. Isaiah sees the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah bringing gold and incense to Zion, so the sons sent away eastward are not finally forgotten.

pos: n. (proper name; a Horite chief, son of Dishon)
etymology: Hebrew 'Eshban, perhaps man of understanding; the meaning is uncertain.
biblical_def: Eshban is a son of Dishon the Horite: “And these are the children of Dishon; Hemdan, and Eshban, and Ithran, and Cheran” (Genesis 36:26). The Horites were the people of Seir before Esau's descendants took the land: “These are the sons of Seir the Horite, who inhabited the land” (Genesis 36:20). Their genealogy is preserved inside Edom's because the two peoples merged; Esau married Aholibamah, a daughter of Anah the Horite. Moses later used the Horites as a lesson for Israel: the LORD had given Seir to Esau and dispossessed the Horims before him, just as He would give Canaan to Israel (Deuteronomy 2:12). Eshban is a name in that displaced people. His record shows that the LORD sets the bounds of every nation, and that Israel's inheritance was not unique in being a gift; it was unique in being covenant.

pos: n. (proper name; a Horite chief, eldest son of Dishon)
etymology: Hebrew Chemdan, pleasant or desirable, from chamad, to desire, to delight in.
biblical_def: Hemdan is the firstborn of Dishon the Horite: “And these are the children of Dishon; Hemdan, and Eshban, and Ithran, and Cheran” (Genesis 36:26). In the Chronicler's parallel the King James text reads Amram: “And the sons of Dishon; Amram, and Eshban, and Ithran, and Cheran” (1 Chronicles 1:41), and the translators' margin notes that the two are the same man; the Hebrew forms differ by a single similar letter. He is not Amram the father of Moses, who was a Levite of the house of Kohath centuries later. Hemdan's name comes from chamad, the verb of the tenth commandment, thou shalt not covet, and of the tree that was pleasant to the eyes and to be desired. It names the same faculty of delight that can fasten on God's gifts rightly or on forbidden things wrongly. Hemdan himself is only a name among the chiefs of a displaced people.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Gad, father of the Haggites)
etymology: Hebrew Chaggi, festive or born on a feast, from chag, feast, festival.
biblical_def: Haggi is the second son of Gad, who went down into Egypt with Jacob: “And the sons of Gad; Ziphion, and Haggi, Shuni, and Ezbon, Eri, and Arodi, and Areli” (Genesis 46:16). In the census on the plains of Moab his descendants are counted as a family of their own: “of Haggi, the family of the Haggites” (Numbers 26:15). The tribe of Gad then numbered “forty thousand and five hundred” (Numbers 26:18). His name is the same root as the prophet Haggai's and as chag, the pilgrim feasts of Israel, and it may mean that he was born on a feast day. Gad's blessing from Jacob was a warrior's: “Gad, a troop shall overcome him: but he shall overcome at the last” (Genesis 49:19). Haggi's family was part of that troop, settled east of Jordan, often pressed by enemies and, in the end, carried away by Assyria.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Gad, and a Benjamite son of Bela)
biblical_def: Ezbon is the name of two men. The first is a son of Gad: “And the sons of Gad; Ziphion, and Haggi, Shuni, and Ezbon, Eri, and Arodi, and Areli” (Genesis 46:16). In the census of Numbers 26 his place is taken by Ozni, “Of Ozni, the family of the Oznites” (Numbers 26:16), and the King James margin notes that the two are the same man. The second Ezbon is a Benjamite: “And the sons of Bela; Ezbon, and Uzzi, and Uzziel, and Jerimoth, and Iri, five; heads of the house of their fathers, mighty men of valour” (1 Chronicles 7:7). Two tribes and two lists, Gad's settlers in Gilead and Benjamin's men of valour, share the name. Neither is remembered for any act. Each is remembered as a head of a house, for Scripture reckons Israel by families before it reckons it by deeds.

corruption_summary: Variant names in parallel lists are offered as proof of error; they are the ordinary marks of men known by more than one name.
corruption_paragraphs: That Gad's son is Ezbon in Genesis and Ozni in Numbers is sometimes cited against the reliability of the record. Men in the ancient world, as now, were known by more than one name, and the King James translators noted the identity in the margin rather than hiding it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture's genealogies are records of real households, preserved with care. A difference of name between two lists is evidence of independent sources faithfully kept, not of carelessness.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Etsbon, meaning uncertain; a son of Gad (Ozni), and a Benjamite head of house.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Etsbon; the meaning is uncertain.
A son of Gad who went down into Egypt (Genesis 46:16).
Called Ozni, father of the Oznites, in Numbers 26:16.
A son of Bela the Benjamite (1 Chronicles 7:7).
The Benjamite was a head of his father's house.
usage: the sons of Bela; Ezbon, and Uzzi
